description.text: Paul Joseph Jean Poupard was born on 30 August 1930 in the small town of Bouzillé in the Maine‑et‑Loire department of France. He entered the minor seminary in Beaupréau and later studied at the University of Angers before completing doctorates in theology and history at the Sorbonne’s École Pratique des Hautes Études. Ordained a priest on 18 December 1954 by Bishop Stanislas Courbe, he taught at the Mongazon School and entered the French section of the Secretariat of State in 1959, where he rose through the ranks to become Chaplain of His Holiness in 1965 and Honorary Prelate in 1971.

Poupard’s curial career spanned more than a quarter of a century. After serving as Rector of the Institut Catholique de Paris (1972‑1980) and vice‑president of the Society of French Ecclesiastical History, he was appointed Auxiliary Bishop of Paris in 1979 and consecrated that April. In 1980 he became Pro‑President of the Secretariat for Non‑Believers, which was renamed the Pontifical Council for Culture in 1988; he led that council as President from 1988 until 2007, a tenure that saw the council’s engagement with contemporary art, science and technology. Elevated to the College of Cardinals in 1985, he later presided briefly over the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue from March 2006 until September 2007, and he participated as a cardinal elector in the 2005 conclave that elected Pope Benedict XVI.

curiosities.text: Poupard’s writings have been translated into more than a dozen languages, including Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Russian, reflecting his broad engagement with global audiences.

He has received honorary doctorates from universities across the world, such as the University of Kyoto in Japan, the University of Santiago de Chile, and Babes‑Bolyai University in Cluj‑Napoca, Romania.

During his nearly twenty‑year presidency of the Pontifical Council for Culture, Poupard oversaw the council’s involvement in major cultural events, including the Vatican’s participation in the Venice Biennale and the establishment of the Pontifical Academy for Culture.
